title: Part 1, Chapter 4
paragraphs: About what happened to our knight when he left the inn

Day was breaking when Don Quixote left the inn, so happy, so cheerful, so exhilarated at finding himself a knight at last that his joy was about to burst his horse-girths. But recalling his host's advice about the necessities he ought to carry — especially money and shirts — he decided to ride home, supply himself with all of that, and pick up a squire as well; he had in mind a farm-labourer, a neighbour of his, a poor man with a family, but well qualified to act as squire to a knight. With this in mind he turned his horse's head towards his village, and Rocinante, reminded of his old quarters, stepped out so briskly he seemed scarcely to touch the ground.

He had not gone far when out of a thicket on his right there came what sounded like the faint cries of someone in distress, and the moment he heard them he exclaimed, "Thanks be to heaven for the favour it grants me, in offering me so soon an opportunity to fulfil the obligation I have taken on and reap the fruits of my ambition. These cries, no doubt, come from some man or woman in need of help — needing my aid and protection;" and wheeling, he turned Rocinante in the direction the cries seemed to come from. He had gone only a few paces into the wood when he saw a mare tied to an oak, and tied to another tree, stripped to the waist, a youth of about fifteen, from whom the cries were coming. Nor were they without cause, for a hefty farmer was flogging him with a belt and following up every blow with scoldings and orders, repeating, "Keep your mouth shut and your eyes open!" while the boy kept answering, "I won't do it again, master; by God's passion I won't do it again, and I'll watch the flock more carefully next time."

Seeing what was going on, Don Quixote said in an angry voice, "Discourteous knight, it ill becomes you to attack one who cannot defend himself; mount your steed and take your lance" (for there was a lance leaning against the oak the mare was tied to), "and I will make you understand that what you are doing is the behaviour of a coward." The farmer, seeing this figure in full armour brandishing a lance over his head, gave himself up for dead, and answered meekly, "Sir Knight, this boy I am chastising is my servant, hired by me to watch a flock of sheep nearby; he is so careless that I lose one every day, and when I punish him for his carelessness and dishonesty he says I do it out of stinginess, to dodge paying him the wages I owe him — and before God, on my soul, he lies."

"Lies to my face, you base clown!" said Don Quixote. "By the sun that shines on us I have a mind to run you through with this lance. Pay him at once and not another word; or, by the God that rules us, I will make an end of you and wipe you out on the spot. Release him this instant."
The farmer hung his head, and without a word untied his servant, of whom Don Quixote asked how much his master owed him.
He answered, nine months at seven reals a month. Don Quixote did the arithmetic, found it came to sixty-three reals, and told the farmer to pay it down at once if he didn't want to die for it.

The trembling clown answered that, as he lived and by the oath he had sworn (though he had sworn no such oath), it was not that much; account had to be taken — and deducted — for three pairs of shoes he had given him, and a real for two bloodlettings when he was sick.

"That's all very well," said Don Quixote, "but let the shoes and the bloodlettings stand as a setoff against the beatings you have given him without any cause; for if he wore out the leather of the shoes you paid for, you have damaged the leather of his body, and if the barber drew blood from him when he was sick, you have drawn it when he was healthy. On that score he owes you nothing."
"The difficulty is, Sir Knight, that I have no money on me here; let Andres come home with me and I will pay him every last real."
"Go with him!" cried the boy. "God forbid! No, señor, not for the world; for once alone with me, he'd flay me like Saint Bartholomew."

"He will do nothing of the kind," said Don Quixote; "I have only to command, and he will obey me; and since he has sworn to me by the order of knighthood he has received, I leave him free, and I guarantee the payment."
"Think about what you're saying, señor," said the boy; "this master of mine is not a knight, nor has he received any order of knighthood; he is Juan Haldudo the Rich, of Quintanar."
"That matters little," replied Don Quixote; "there may well be Haldudo knights; besides, every man is the son of his own deeds."
"That's true," said Andres; "but this master of mine — of what deeds is he the son, when he refuses me the wages of my sweat and labour?"

"I don't refuse, brother Andres," said the farmer, "just be good enough to come along with me, and I swear by all the orders of knighthood there are in the world to pay you what was agreed, real by real, and perfumed."

"I'll excuse you the perfume," said Don Quixote; "give it to him in reals and I'll be satisfied; and see that you do as you have sworn. If not, by the same oath I swear to come back and hunt you down and punish you; and I will find you, though you hide closer than a lizard. And if you want to know who lays this command on you, so that you are the more firmly bound to obey, know that I am the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, the undoer of wrongs and injustices; and so, God be with you, and don't forget what you have promised and sworn, under the penalties already declared to you."

Saying this, he spurred Rocinante and was soon out of reach. The farmer followed him with his eyes, and once he saw that he had cleared the wood and was out of sight, he turned to his boy Andres and said, "Come here, son, I want to pay you what I owe you, just as that undoer of wrongs commanded me."

"My oath on it," said Andres, "your worship will be wise to obey the command of that good knight — may he live a thousand years — for as he is a valiant and just judge, by Roque, if you do not pay me he will come back and do as he said."

"My oath on it too," said the farmer; "but as I have such a strong affection for you, I want to add to the debt so I can add to the payment;" and seizing him by the arm, he tied him up again and gave him such a flogging that he left him for dead.

"Now, Master Andres," said the farmer, "call on the undoer of wrongs; you'll find he won't undo that — though I'm not sure I'm quite done with you, since I have a good mind to flay you alive." But in the end he untied him and let him go look for his judge, so the sentence could be put into execution.

Andres set off rather down in the mouth, swearing he would go and find the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha and tell him exactly what had happened, and that all of it would have to be repaid sevenfold; but for all that, he went off weeping, while his master stood laughing.

Thus did the valiant Don Quixote right that wrong, and, thoroughly pleased with how the whole thing had turned out, considering that he had made a very happy and noble beginning to his knighthood, he took the road towards his village in perfect self-content, saying under his breath, "Well may you today call yourself fortunate above all on earth, O Dulcinea del Toboso, fairest of the fair! since it has fallen to your lot to hold subject and submissive to your full will and pleasure a knight so renowned as is, and will be, Don Quixote of La Mancha — who, as all the world knows, only yesterday received the order of knighthood and today has righted the greatest wrong and grievance that ever injustice conceived and cruelty perpetrated; who has today snatched the rod from the hand of that ruthless oppressor so wantonly lashing that tender child."

He now came to a road branching in four directions, and at once he was reminded of those crossroads where knights-errant used to halt to consider which road to take. In imitation of them he stopped for a while, and after deep deliberation he gave Rocinante his head, deferring his own will to that of his hack, who followed out his first intention — making straight for his own stable. After he had gone about two miles, Don Quixote noticed a large party of people, who, as it turned out, were some Toledo traders on their way to buy silk at Murcia. There were six of them coming along under their sunshades, with four mounted servants and three muleteers on foot. The moment Don Quixote spotted them, the fancy seized him that here must be some new adventure; and to help him imitate as nearly as he could the episodes he had read about in his books, this seemed sent expressly for the purpose, and he resolved to take it on. So with a lofty bearing and resolve he planted his feet firmly in the stirrups, got his lance ready, brought his buckler up to his chest, and, planting himself in the middle of the road, stood waiting for these knights-errant to approach — for that is what he now considered and held them to be. When they had come near enough to see and hear, he cried out with a haughty gesture, "All the world stand, unless all the world will confess that in all the world there is no maiden fairer than the Empress of La Mancha, the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso."

The traders halted at this language and the sight of the strange figure delivering it, and from both figure and language they at once guessed the craziness of the speaker; but they wanted to find out quietly what was the point of this confession demanded of them, and one of them, who was fond of a joke and quite quick-witted, said, "Sir Knight, we do not know who this good lady is that you speak of; show her to us, for if she is of such beauty as you suggest, with all our hearts and without any pressure we will confess the truth that you require of us."

"If I were to show her to you," replied Don Quixote, "what credit would there be in your confessing a truth so self-evident? The essential point is that, without seeing her, you must believe, confess, affirm, swear, and defend it; if not, you have me to deal with in battle, ill-conditioned, arrogant rabble that you are. Come at me, one by one as the order of knighthood requires, or all together, as is the custom and vile habit of your kind — here I stand and wait for you, relying on the justice of the cause I uphold."

"Sir Knight," replied the trader, "I beg your worship, in the name of this present company of princes, that to spare us from burdening our consciences with the confession of a thing we have never seen or heard of — and one moreover so much to the prejudice of the Empresses and Queens of the Alcarria and Estremadura — your worship will be pleased to show us some portrait of this lady, even if it be no bigger than a grain of wheat; for by the thread one finds the ball, and that way we'll be satisfied and easy, and you'll be content and pleased. In fact I think we are already so far in agreement with you that even if her portrait showed her blind in one eye, and oozing vermilion and sulphur out of the other, we would, to oblige your worship, still say everything in her favour you could desire."

"She oozes nothing of the kind, you vile rabble," said Don Quixote, burning with rage. "Nothing of the kind, I say — only ambergris and civet in cotton wool; nor is she one-eyed or humpbacked, but straighter than a Guadarrama spindle. But you shall pay for the blasphemy you have uttered against beauty like that of my lady."

And with that, he charged with levelled lance at the man who had spoken, with such fury and ferocity that if luck had not arranged for Rocinante to stumble and fall midway, it would have gone badly for the reckless trader. Down went Rocinante, and over went his master, rolling along the ground for some distance; and when he tried to get up he couldn't, so encumbered was he with lance, buckler, spurs, helmet, and the weight of his old armour. All the while he was struggling to rise, he kept shouting, "Don't run, you cowards and wretches! Stand and fight, for it's not my fault but my horse's that I'm stretched here."

One of the muleteers in the party, who could not have had much good nature in him, hearing the poor man on the ground blustering like this, could not resist giving him an answer on his ribs; and coming up to him, he seized the lance, broke it into pieces, and with one of them began thrashing our Don Quixote so thoroughly that, in spite of his armour, he ground him like a measure of wheat. His masters called out not to lay on so hard and to leave the man alone, but the muleteer's blood was up, and he wasn't dropping the game until he had vented the rest of his rage, and gathering up the remaining fragments of the lance, he finished by hammering them down on the unhappy victim, who all through the storm of sticks that rained on him never stopped threatening heaven, and earth, and the brigands, as they seemed to him. At last the muleteer was tired, and the traders went on their way, taking with them plenty to talk about, in the matter of the poor fellow who had been cudgelled. As for him, finding himself alone, he made another effort to rise; but if he hadn't been able when whole and sound, how was he to rise after being thrashed and well-nigh knocked to pieces? And yet he counted himself lucky, since to his mind this was a regular knight-errant's mishap, and entirely, in his view, the fault of his horse. However, battered in body as he was, getting up was beyond his power.
